sections.html:
Xenia is the Greene County seat, about 15 miles east of Dayton in the Miami Valley, and storms shaped its housing history. An F5 tornado crossed the middle of the city on April 3, 1974, killing 34 people and destroying almost half of the city's buildings. Another tornado, rated F4, hit on September 20, 2000. The city keeps a system of tornado sirens.

A seller who can hand a buyer receipts for a recent roof, siding or storm repair has useful paperwork, because storm history is an obvious question in Xenia.

The market sits between a college-town market and a heavily rental city. Population is an estimated 26,425, a 3.8% gain on the 25,447 counted in 2020. Figures for 2020 to 2024 follow.

  • Owner-occupied rate: 60.9%, with a median owner-occupied value of $162,400.
  • Median gross rent: $931.
  • 10,765 households averaging 2.32 people.
  • 22.4% of residents are under 18, and 20.4% are 65 or older.
  • Mean travel time to work is 24.6 minutes, and the city's website carries a page for people relocating to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
  • Median household income is $56,029.

Xenia sits in a transportation triangle formed by I-70, I-71 and I-75, reached by U.S. 35, U.S. 42 and U.S. 68. A listing can state the highway access plainly, since buyers who drive to Dayton or beyond will check it.

Xenia Community Schools serves the city, and private options include Legacy Christian Academy and St. Brigid School. Confirm which building serves your address before you list.

The Little Miami Scenic Trail runs through Xenia Station, and the city carries the nickname "Bicycle Capital of the Midwest," since five of its six former rail roadbeds have been converted to trail use. The Greene County Fairgrounds hosts the annual Dayton Hamvention, which typically draws more than 20,000 amateur radio enthusiasts. If your house sits near the fairgrounds, mention the event traffic in your showing notes so buyers aren't surprised.

Planning and Zoning issues zoning permits and also enforces the property maintenance code, the city's floor for safe, sanitary buildings. The division works from the City Administration Building at 107 East Main Street, weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m., and takes calls at 937-372-6389.

Two practical points for sellers:

  • The city's project list includes a "Zoning Update 2026." Ask Planning and Zoning whether the update changes the rules for your lot, an addition or an accessory building before you promise a buyer a particular use.
  • Code enforcement is separate from the Building Division. Answer a notice about tall grass, debris or a failing structure before the house goes on the market.

Planning and Zoning sits under the Development Services Department, the place to start with a question about an unpermitted porch, deck or garage.

sections.h2: How Greene County values a house and when you can appeal
sections.html:
The Greene County Auditor values property by mass appraisal, building a table from sales data in each area and testing it against actual sales. Ohio doesn't allow foreclosure sales in that analysis because they aren't arm's-length sales, so a distressed sale next door shouldn't drag your value down in the county's model.

A triennial update happens every three years without a visual inspection, and a full revaluation with a physical review happens in the sixth year. An owner who thinks the appraisal is too high may file with the Greene County Board of Revision, and the window runs January 1 to March 31. There's no dollar-for-dollar link between a change in value and a change in taxes, because the voted levies are applied to the value.

Homestead rules and income limits change over time, so ask the Greene County Auditor for the current application and limits.

sections.h2: Tax relief after a tornado or fire
sections.html:
Ohio Revised Code 323.17 gives the county board of revision a specific tool. If fire, flood, a tornado or another cause destroys or damages taxable property by 25% or more of its listed value, and at least $2,000 of taxable value, the board may pass a resolution pushing the payment deadline back by as much as a year.

Copies go to the auditor and treasurer along with the board's damage estimate. Owners selling a storm-damaged house should ask the Greene County Auditor how to request an extension and tell the title company, so the settlement statement shows what remains unpaid.

Three offices touch a Xenia deed. A notary or another listed official takes the owner's acknowledgment (ORC 5301.01), the Greene County Auditor endorses the conveyance once the buyer files a value statement and the seller pays the conveyance fee (ORC 319.202), and the recorder then files it. A deed left unrecorded can lose to a later buyer who had no notice (ORC 5301.25).

sections.h2: When a cash offer makes sense
sections.html:
A cash offer suits a Xenia house that a lender's appraiser would mark down, such as one with worn shingles, a wet basement or storm repairs never finished. Owners who inherited a house or manage a rental from out of town also use it.

Get each offer in writing with the closing date and the party responsible for closing costs. Set the figures beside what a regular listing would net after commission and repairs, and ask the title company for a draft settlement statement early.

sections.h2: A practical order for a quick sale
sections.html:
Begin with the paperwork on the house. Gather receipts for roof, siding and storm repairs, and check with Planning and Zoning about any porch, deck or garage built without a permit. Clear any notice about grass, debris or a failing structure.

Then line up the deed. Find a notary, plan for the value statement the buyer files with the auditor, and budget for the conveyance fee, which is the seller's cost. Ask the title company to prepare the settlement statement early so you can see what remains unpaid, especially if a tornado or fire damaged the house and a tax extension is in play.

A cash buyer can skip the lender's appraisal and any repair demands, which helps when a house needs work. The county steps stay the same for every kind of sale, and a deed that isn't recorded promptly can lose out to a later buyer.

faqs.q: Does Xenia's tornado history change how I should sell?
faqs.a: It changes what buyers ask. The April 1974 F5 and the September 2000 F4 are well known, so keep receipts for roof, siding and storm repairs and hand them over early. The city also keeps a siren system, which some buyers ask about.

faqs.q: Does Greene County count a foreclosure sale when it sets values?
faqs.a: No. Ohio doesn't allow foreclosure sales in the county's analysis because they aren't arm's-length sales. Ordinary sales in your area are what the appraisal tables are tested against.

faqs.q: Is my Xenia house covered by a tax extension if a tornado damaged it?
faqs.a: Possibly. Section 323.17 lets the Greene County board of revision grant up to a year more to pay when the loss reaches 25% of listed value and $2,000 of taxable value. Ask the auditor how to apply.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about zoning for a house in Xenia?
faqs.a: Phone Planning and Zoning at 937-372-6389 or stop by 107 East Main Street on a weekday between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. Raise the Zoning Update 2026 project if the property has an addition or a second building.

faqs.q: How long can I wait to appeal my Greene County value?
faqs.a: The county takes complaints from January 1 until March 31 each year. The board looks at value only, so the voted levy rates stay as they are.
